ranks.rationale:
k183 is the most distinctive and best crafted. It works as one idea: an old-style technical engraving, with each sign as a numbered "Fig." showing a cutaway of the water heater and a magnified detail (corroded anode, scale at the bottom of the tank, dripping safety valve, rating plate with the manufacture date circled, scaled-up heating element). Each slide splits into "Le signe" and "À faire", and a footer tracker fills in as you swipe. The serif typography is refined, it signals craft and a family business since 1987, and the CTA (49 €, "offert si remplacement", 3 générations, 9 techniciens, 7j/7, phone number, website) is complete. It covers the whole brief and reads well at 1080x1350.

k154 is the strongest of the navy/copper "clean flat" group. Its diagrams are really educational: labelled Anode, Résistance, Calcaire, Molette and Évacuation, a plate reading "Fab. 03/2013" next to an age gauge, and a chart linking millimetres of scale to extra consumption. Each slide has a severity marker ("À traiter vite", "À surveiller"), and the offer slide is clear, with what the diagnostic covers.

k112 is close behind. The cover is strong, with chips for the 5 signs. Illustrations are good (tap and thermometer, a "CLAC!" tank, gouttes = OK vs filet = alerte), each slide has clear "Pourquoi / Quoi faire" cards, sign 4 uses a big "10+ ans" treatment, and the CTA has trust stats. It feels slightly more generic than k154.

k156 is very similar and polished: an annotated cover, a Normal / Pas normal split on sign 3, and a lifespan bar. Its outlined numbers and the familiar template put it a bit below the two above.

k105 is solid and punchy, with a navy/red/mustard palette, "TOC TOC BLOUB" and a "+30 %" chart. Its icons are cruder and the all-caps heavy type is less refined.

k128 is clean and readable in condensed caps with orange accents. The illustrations are simple (glass of rusty water, calendar showing "10+"), which makes it competent but generic.

k109 puts signs 4 and 5 on a single cramped slide to make room for two offer and contact slides. That breaks the one-sign-per-slide rhythm. Its illustrations are minimal (a drop, a sound icon).

k134 comes last. The pressure-gauge concept is clever, but it repeats the same gauge on all 7 slides, so the visuals barely change. The "À faire" advice is thin ("Demandez un diagnostic"), and the cover has visible defects: the circumflex on "LÂCHER" collides with the line above it, and the needle runs over the numeral 5.

What separates the top from the bottom: the top pieces have an illustration made for each sign that actually teaches something and fits the brand story, while the bottom ones rely on a generic template, repeat visuals, compress content, or show typographic collisions.
